item.title: Yatra’s ‘MICE’ Problem
item.dc:creator: Gargi Sarkar
item.description: Bookings grew, but revenue shrank and profit disappeared. That was the paradox of Yatra in the September quarter, when India’s…
item.content:encoded:
Bookings grew, but revenue shrank and profit disappeared. That was the paradox of Yatra in the September quarter, when India’s travel tech sector was expected to capture the momentum leading into the festive and holiday travel season.

The listed travel tech company reported a consolidated net loss of ₹78.4 Lakh in Q2 FY27, against a net profit of ₹14.3 Cr in the year-ago period. 

Revenue from operations declined 39.1% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹213.6 Cr, reflecting a slowdown in its ‘Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions’ (MICE) business, which has historically contributed meaningfully to its corporate travel operations.

Yatra’s results have come at a precarious time. Its US-listed parent, Yatra Online, has received a notice from the Nasdaq for failing to maintain the exchange’s minimum $1 closing bid-price requirement. 

Separately, the Indian-listed entity’s shares have remained under pressure due to factors like earnings growth, business visibility and the ability to convert booking growth into profitability.

Interestingly, Yatra’s gross bookings rose 6% YoY to ₹2,165.5 Cr during the quarter, leaving the OTA grappling with a peculiar paradox: rising booking volumes but shrinking revenue and profitability.

So, why is Yatra struggling to make more money despite a growth in bookings? And is the MICE slowdown the only problem or is there more? 

MICE Crushes Revenue Growth

At first glance, Yatra’s 39% revenue decline appears steep, particularly when compared with the growth reported by some of its online travel peers. Yatra attributed the revenue decline primarily to lower revenue from MICE, which is recognised on a gross basis. 

For context, ixigo reported a 13% YoY increase in revenue from operations to ₹320.96 Cr in Q2 FY27, while its gross transaction value (GTV) grew 22%. Similarly, MakeMyTrip reported 11.2% revenue growth in constant currency to $232.5 Mn, with gross bookings rising 20.9%. 

Yatra’s gross bookings, by comparison, grew only by 5.6% YoY to ₹2,165.5 Cr. Profitability also remained a concern. Adjusted EBITDA declined 41.2% YoY to ₹15 Cr, while the company reported a small net loss of ₹78 Lakh.

Pressure was visible across its business segments. Gross bookings from air ticketing business rose 15% to ₹1,700.6 Cr, while air gross margin rose 29% to ₹75.7 Cr and air ticketing adjusted margin improved by 20.8%. While standalone hotel gross bookings grew 20%, the losses in the hotels and packages business continued to drag down the gains from air ticketing.

The company’s H1 FY27 operating cash flow turned negative at ₹14.7 Cr, primarily because of a ₹48.8 Cr working capital deployment. 

This is worth tracking alongside its reported profitability, particularly as the company continues to invest in technology and expand its corporate customer base. Yatra had cash, cash equivalents and term deposits of approximately ₹218 Cr at the end of September 2026. 

Unlike consumer-facing travel platforms that rely heavily on consumer air ticketing, and hotels and holiday bookings, Yatra has a sizeable corporate travel business. It is also one of India’s largest managed corporate travel providers, with MICE driving these bookings. This should provide a relatively stable source of bookings compared to discretionary leisure travel.

During Q2 FY27, the company added 54 corporate customers, with an annual billable potential of ₹203.5 Cr. Corporate bookings grew 18% YoY and 10% sequentially, while 54% of existing corporate clients increased their spending.

Personal travel bookings by employees of corporate clients also increased 36% YoY, pointing to opportunities for cross-selling within its existing customer base. This is significant because corporate travel relationships can generate repeat bookings and provide access to a wider employee base. 

Nasdaq’s Compliance Pressure

The earnings pressure is not the only issue confronting Yatra’s investors. On November 10, the US-listed parent of Yatra Online Ltd received a notification from Nasdaq’s listing qualifications department after its ordinary shares failed to maintain the minimum $1 closing bid price for the required period.

According to the notice, the company’s shares did not meet the minimum bid-price requirement between September 29 and November 9, 2026, under Nasdaq listing rules.

The company has been given 180 calendar days, i.e. until May 10, 2027, to get back in compliance. To do so, its shares must close at $1 or higher for at least 10 consecutive business days, or longer (generally up to 20 consecutive business days). This can be further extended by 180 days if Yatra fails to meet the compliance requirements, subject to other listing-related requirements. 

But Yatra does run the risk of getting delisted in May next year if it fails on any of Nasdaq’s criteria. 

A reverse stock split is among the options the company could consider to restore compliance. However, Yatra has cautioned that there is no assurance it will regain compliance or qualify for an additional period.

“The notice concerns the US-listed parent and should not be confused with a separate delisting warning for Yatra Online Ltd’s shares on the BSE and NSE. Nevertheless, the development adds to the pressure surrounding the broader Yatra group. Investors will take full context into the picture as its performance on the Indian stock market has also been very weak,” an analyst tracking travel stocks said.

Travel Stocks Tumble

Yatra’s stock performance is also part of a broader correction across India’s listed travel and travel tech companies. Most consumer-facing travel platforms have struggled to sustain their valuations in 2026.

As of November 13, 2026, Yatra Online’s shares had declined approximately 56% year-to-date (YTD), making it one of the worst performers among listed travel tech companies. Its shares closed at ₹77.64 on the BSE on November 13, against a 52-week high of ₹201.85.

Le Travenues Technology, the parent of Ixigo, had fallen approximately 34% YTD, while Easy Trip Planners was down around 24%. Both companies have faced pressure on profitability and valuation concerns.

The correction extends to larger travel stocks as well. IRCTC has declined approximately 35% YTD, while Thomas Cook India is down around 25-29%, despite these businesses having considerable differences. 

“The broader correction suggests that investors are becoming more selective about travel-related stocks. While India’s travel market continues to benefit from rising discretionary spending and online booking adoption, companies are being evaluated on their ability to sustain margins, improve monetisation and generate consistent earnings,” the analyst quoted above said.

What Could Fix Yatra

For Yatra, the next few quarters will be important in establishing whether the Q2 weakness was largely a temporary MICE-related disruption or indicative of more persistent pressure on its corporate travel business.

But there were some early signs of improvement in the MICE business which could bode well for the third quarter. For example, bookings recovered 37% sequentially as corporates began rescheduling programmes that had been deferred or scaled down. This, however, is yet to translate into a meaningful improvement in earnings.

Yatra is also betting on SME and mid-market customers, technology-led automation and expense management solutions to expand its addressable market.

However, investors will want to see these initiatives translate into better topline and operating leverage on the corporate travel and events front to shore up margins. The company will also need to demonstrate that it can manage corporate travel demand volatility with each passing season. For now, Yatra has a MICE problem but not a lot of solutions.

item.title: EaseMyTrip Q2: Loss Narrows 98% YoY To ₹57 Lakh, Revenue Up 34%
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Online travel aggregator (OTA) EaseMyTrip managed to narrow its consolidated net loss by 98.4% to ₹56.5 Lakh in the second…
item.content:encoded:
Online travel aggregator (OTA) EaseMyTrip managed to narrow its consolidated net loss by 98.4% to ₹56.5 Lakh in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) compared to a loss of ₹36 Cr in the year-ago quarter. 

On a sequential basis, the company also managed to trim its losses by 95.2% from ₹11.7 Cr in Q1 FY27.

The shrinking loss came as the OTA’s operating revenue zoomed 33.5% to ₹157.9 Cr during the quarter under review from ₹118.3 Cr in Q2 FY26. On a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) basis, the startup’s top line also rose 17.3% from ₹134.7 Cr in the preceding June quarter.

Including other income of ₹10 Cr, EaseMyTrip’s total income stood at ₹168 Cr in the quarter under review.

Meanwhile, total expenses also surged 36.5% to ₹164.2 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹120.3 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Service costs soared 169.9% YoY to nearly ₹40 Cr in the quarter ended September 2026, while employee benefit expenses rose a marginal 2.4% to ₹31.9 Cr.

Overall, the uptick in the OTA’s top line was driven by its hotel packages business. As per its financial statements, the segment’s revenue surged 189% YoY to ₹92 Cr in Q2 FY27. However, the company’s air passage revenue declined 21.9% YoY to ₹56.3 Cr, while other services’ top line tanked 33.1% YoY to ₹9.6 Cr in the quarter under review. 

In its investor presentation, EMT also claimed that its quarterly hotel night bookings zoomed 87.5% YoY to 7.9 Lakh in Q2 FY27, while the trains, buses, and others segment recorded a 39% YoY decline in transactions to 2 Lakh.

Overall, the OTA claimed that its gross booking revenue (GBR) grew 25.5% to ₹2,458.4 Cr in Q2 FY27 as against ₹1,958.7 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year.

Flights still accounted for the biggest chunk of EMT’s total GBR in Q2 FY27 at 69.6%, while hotels and holiday packages brought in 28.9%. Trains, buses and other services made up the remaining 1.4%.

In a statement, EaseMyTrip also noted that its Dubai operations continued to see strong business momentum during the quarter.

The OTA’s Dubai operations clocked a GBR of ₹556 Cr in Q1 FY27, up 53.6% from ₹362 Cr in Q2 FY26.

Going forward, the company said that it plans to focus on diversification, international expansion and AI-led “innovation”.

“… The company is also pursuing international growth opportunities through corporate partnerships, including initiatives in Latin America, Brazil, US, UK and Thailand. International expansion remains an important pillar of Vision 2030, providing EaseMyTrip with opportunities to broaden its geographic presence and develop additional sources of business,” added EMT in a statement.

Shares of EMT closed Friday’s trading session 1.01% higher at ₹6.01 apiece on the BSE.

item.title: Not Just About Temple: India’s Wearable Impasse
item.dc:creator: Debarghya Sil
item.description: “There is no established playbook for making wearables in India. If you have the capital, you can set up a…
item.content:encoded:
“There is no established playbook for making wearables in India. If you have the capital, you can set up a team, hire a bunch of researchers and scientists and come up with a product and even start selling it,” a California-based Indian founder of a wearable startup told us this week. 

The heated and contentious battle on X over Temple has brought out a lot into the open. A lot has been said and written about Temple this month, and who’s right and who’s wrong. What has gone unanswered in the cacophony is what it takes to actually launch a health or fitness tracking wearable that’s made in India. 

Where do founders turn when they need their hypothesis tested? Which agencies are the most approachable and how much red tape can one expect? These questions are not just about Temple. It’s about any new device that’s being launched in India, whether it is looking to track blood flow to the brain or it is just a heart rate or fitness monitor. 

The distinction matters in a market where wearable manufacturers can build and sell products that track physiological parameters without necessarily undergoing the clinical validation expected of medical devices. 

For India’s wearable industry, the debate has exposed gaps in how companies develop, validate and market products that make health-related claims or even basic activity tracking. But first, let’s see where Temple stands before diving deeper into the ecosystem of health wearables. 

Temple’s Bet On Something New 

Deepinder Goyal launched Temple with a core proposition of tracking blood flow to the brain and entropy. The company set out to create two new metrics that give users something their smartwatches could never.

Firstly, BrainFlow is said to track relative changes in the blood flow to the brain during everyday activity. On the other hand, Goyal has described Entropy as a measure of how hard the body works to shed heat. 

The company’s website says the metric captures the body’s load across thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive, emotional, pharmacological, postural, reproductive and recovery systems. However, research papers uploaded on its website clearly state that Temple cannot directly measure cerebral blood flow. 

In response to Inc42’s questions about how these are measured, Temple said the Brain Flow Index is a relative index derived from optical signals collected at the temple. The company said the index rose and fell alongside blood-flow velocity in the middle cerebral artery, a major artery in the brain, as measured through transcranial Doppler ultrasound.

Temple said the metric currently has two applications in its fitness app. It helps users compare the intensity of their cardio sessions and sends prompts to move when their Brain Flow Index drops during long periods of sitting.

Unlike heart rate or sleep tracking, which have been part of consumer wearables for years, Entropy is being positioned as a new physiological metric. Its scientific validity will depend on whether the underlying signals can reliably measure what the company claims. 

The fact that Temple is broaching new territory with these metrics is what has set alarm bells ringing. Founders we spoke to say most wearables already have algorithms available for the heart rate and sleep tracking that have been improved and enhanced over the years since the first such devices came about. 

“The real work comes when you develop a new tracker or establish a new biomarker or a new benchmark for measuring something new,” the founder quoted at the beginning said, adding that specialised algorithms need research papers and validation. 

This is why there’s so much scepticism around Temple in the medical fraternity, with many doctors accusing the company of pushing a product without adequate backing. 

Temple’s research page lists multiple studies examining its BrainFlow technology, including a study involving 23 healthy adults that compared its reading with transcranial Doppler (TCD), a clinical technique used to measure blood-flow velocity in major brain arteries. 

Another study compared Temple’s BrainFlow readings with near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), a technique that can distinguish blood volume changes in the brain from those in the scalp.

The company says it has partnered with academic institutions across the world to study additional and more diverse groups of people, with further validation studies underway.

Both studies are listed as being under peer review. A Temple spokesperson told Inc42 that validation work on Entropy is in its final stages and that it plans to publish the findings soon. 

Of Preprints And Peer Reviews

After much criticism, on November 8, Goyal acknowledged the gap between the peer reviews, the studies and the launch of the devices, adding that the research on Entropy would be published soon. He also said BrainFlow was not the primary proposition behind Temple, but the starting point for its research. 

In an earlier November 5 post, Goyal said preprints would precede peer-reviewed publication and that further validation would continue as the product reached users. 

The distinction between publishing a white paper, uploading a preprint and completing peer review matters. But what do these words mean for founders who are entering the space fresh? 

Simply put, a white paper and a preprint make research available for public scrutiny, while peer review brings an independent assessment of the methodology, findings and conclusions. 

A second founder, an early stage entrepreneur building neuro-centric wearables, said credible validation requires controlled trials. “Generally, you need a double-blind test, a control group and a placebo group. The bare minimum that is respectable enough is 90 people.” 

However, there is no fixed requirement on the number of participants, they said when we asked whether 23 people is a large enough sample size for Temple’s study. “You can do it for 10 people. Nothing is a mandate. But is it respectable to have a big test group? Maybe,” the founder added.

We were also told that publishing research papers is not compulsory either, but it helps establish credibility. At the moment, no regulations govern the release of such papers along with a product. “It’s not necessary to put out your research papers, but it is something that people demand for credibility,” the second founder added. 

Plus, getting a study peer-reviewed is not easy. Founders need to find the right testing bodies to conduct reviews. This comes along with a growing demand for independent validation from investors and others who want to partner with the startup. “Third-party trials are what most wearables get asked for, by investors and consumers. Even doctors are asking for them,” the founder added.

For early stage startups, the cost of conducting larger studies can be a huge constraint. 

In their case, a study comprising just 100 subjects cost the startup around ₹15 Lakh, which the company claims is a lot at the early stage especially when the product has already been built. Most of the funds raised are depleted by the time the startup reaches the testing stage.  

Is Temple A Medical Device? 

The debate also raises questions about how India’s regulatory framework applies to wearable devices. 

Under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, a product’s classification depends on its intended purpose and the function it is designed to perform. 

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) regulates devices intended for purposes such as diagnosing, preventing, monitoring or treating diseases, as well as investigating or modifying physiological processes.

Simply calling a product a fitness or wellness tracker does not settle its regulatory classification. Its intended use, advertised claims and actual functionality matter when it comes to clearances. 

Some well-known doctors in the country, who are sceptical of Temple claims, said the device’s capabilities are not backed ​by peer-reviewed research. Hence, they have called for the device to come under the purview of medical regulators.

However, Goyal has repeatedly maintained that Temple is not a medical device and is not intended to diagnose or prevent any diseases. He has also said that the company will obtain regulatory clearance wherever required before making claims that need it. 

Responding to Inc42, a Temple spokesperson said the device does not diagnose, treat, cure, mitigate or prevent any disease, and makes no claims about any medical condition.

The company argued that under Indian law, a product is classified as a medical device based on its manufacturer’s intended purpose. It also cited CDSCO’s 2026 guidance on medical-device software, which says software intended for general wellness, without any reference to disease, does not fall under the purview of the Medical Devices Rules, 2017.

Temple said that if it ever intends to introduce a feature for a medical purpose, it will seek CDSCO approval before making it available to users.

The Regulatory Road 

Uncertainty extends beyond how companies position their products into what regulatory clearances are needed. 

The second founder, who had earlier spoken about the importance of clinical trials and third-party validation, said their company obtained CDSCO approval despite not making any medical claims. The founder said the company pursued approval because it was developing a brain-focused wearable device.

“In India, any brain wearable device needs CDSCO approval. Whether it is tracking blood flow or not,” the second founder claimed, adding that wearables targeting the brain face additional requirements compared with other wearable devices. “Even though I am not making a medical device, I have a CDSCO clearance. Because it is mandatory in India.”

The approval process in this case stretched around 16 months from November 2024 to March 2026. We were told that before receiving approval, companies can test only a limited number of units in India, with CDSCO determining the permitted number. This also makes it harder for companies to continuously iterate and test. 

The founder was describing their company’s regulatory experience. However, CDSCO’s 2026 guidance on medical device software does not establish a blanket approval requirement for all brain wearables.

The founder acknowledged that rules remain unclear for products positioned as wellness devices. They also pointed to gaps in enforcement, saying regulatory scrutiny is not always consistent. “The CDSCO is not very active in looking into such companies, unfortunately. This is a loophole in India that many exploit,” the founder said.

A third founder said navigating regulatory requirements can be difficult for early stage startups, leading some companies to be over-cautious. “Here you need to play around with the regulatory parts. Because in India the regulations are very hard. The only reason we never say that it is a medical device is that compliance becomes very hard. Especially for a new startup.” 

The founder said companies need to be particularly careful about making claims related to detecting or predicting medical conditions. “So if we say we can detect, then it would be a medical device. So you have to play very carefully with the words.” 

The question, therefore, is whether wearable manufacturers are making claims that bring their products within the scope of medical-device regulation, regardless of how they choose to market them.

Beyond medical device approvals, the founder also highlighted other certifications such as Wireless Planning and Coordination (WPC) approval for relevant equipment that allows wireless connectivity, and Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) certification that are mandatory for electronic devices.

Similarly, the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) framework applies to relevant products marketed in the US and should not be confused with Indian regulatory clearance. Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) certification, meanwhile, relates to an ultra-low-power short-range data transmission over Bluetooth.

The Temple spokesperson told Inc42 that it holds all the certifications required to sell the device in the countries where it is currently available. However, the company did not specify the individual certifications.

Does The Wearable Industry Trust Temple? 

Temple’s development also needs to be viewed in the context of Goyal’s earlier work through Continue research and the Gravity Aging Hypothesis.

The hypothesis explores whether gravity’s long term influence on blood circulation could contribute to aging, particularly through changes in cerebral blood flow. Goyal has previously argued that understanding brain circulation could help researchers investigate longevity and aging. 

Temple emerged from this broader research effort. The device was developed to monitor brain-flow-related signals continuously, giving researchers a way to study physiological changes outside conventional laboratory settings.

However, a hypothesis, a measurable physiological signal and a validated biomarker are all different things. Establishing a relationship between a wearable’s readings and an existing clinical measurement does not automatically demonstrate that the device can predict aging or provide meaningful insights into longevity. 

One of the founders we spoke to said Temple’s placement near the temporal artery was a considered engineering decision, as the location offers a relatively accessible site for optical sensing. However, the founder cautioned that measuring blood flow at the temple does not necessarily establish that a device can measure blood flow within the brain. 

The second founder suggested the strength of Temple’s existing athlete study as a basis for broader performance claims arguing that larger studies involving control groups and independent validation would provide greater confidence. 

For Goyal, the next task is to establish that Temple’s proprietary measurements offer meaningful information beyond existing wearable metrics. 

In his November 8 post, he said consumers were free to wait for peer-reviewed evidence before purchasing the device. He also promised a detailed explanation of how BrainFlow is calculated, its potential application and its limitations. 

The wearable industry does not necessarily need every product to become a medical device; some can remain lifestyle devices. But as manufacturers move beyond counting steps, measuring sleep and tracking heart rates to developing new physiological benchmarks, they will have to show what those numbers actually mean, and how they actually derived it. 

Breakthrough products often begin with a hypothesis. Innovation lies in testing it, learning from the evidence and iterating, while being clear about the outcomes achieved and what remains under study.

Many senior founders and investors have shown faith in Goyal’s ability to build Temple, pointing to his record of building and scaling Zomato and Blinkit (Eternal). Temple is an opportunity for him to bring that experience to a far less proven field: establishing a new category of wearable technology. 

Most importantly, Goyal has shown conviction by committing substantial personal capital to Temple. 

However, its scientific claims will need to withstand independent scrutiny before consumers can judge what the device can deliver.

If Temple can successfully demonstrate that, through continued testing and iteration, it could help create the wearable playbook India lacks.

item.title: DroneAcharya Profits Tank 65% YoY To ₹67 Lakh In H1
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: BSE SME-listed drone tech company DroneAcharya’s net profit plunged 65.3% to ₹67 Lakh in the first half (H1) of the…
item.content:encoded:
BSE SME-listed drone tech company DroneAcharya’s net profit plunged 65.3% to ₹67 Lakh in the first half (H1) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) compared to ₹1.9 Cr in the year-ago period. On a sequential basis, the company had reported a net loss of ₹1.6 Cr in H2 FY26.

The company’s bottom line took a major hit as operating revenue tanked 18.3% to ₹7.8 Cr in the period under review as against ₹9.6 Cr in H1 FY26. However, the top line improved 53.6% sequentially from ₹ 5.1 Cr in the preceding quarter.

Including other income of ₹1.9 Lakh, DroneAcharya’s total income for H1 FY27 stood at ₹7.84 Cr. 

On the operational front, EBITDA stood at ₹4.3 Cr in H1 FY27, a decline of 7.3% from ₹4.6 Cr in the corresponding period last year. However, EBITDA margin improved to 54.7% from 48.2% in H1 FY26.

Founded by Prateek Srivastava in 2017, DroneAcharya manufactures drones. It also offers drone pilot training and mapping services to enterprises. The listed company has also forayed into the defence tech sector and makes kamikaze drones, with plans to launch tethered drones soon.

Where Did Droneacharya Spend?

In H1 FY27, Droneacharya maintained a tight leash on its expenses as total expenditure declined 15.9% YoY to ₹6.9 Cr in H1 FY27. Let’s take a closer look at the company’s spending pattern: 

Employee Benefit Expenses: The company’s personnel costs fell by 13.3% YoY to ₹1.8 Cr in the six month period ended September 2026 from ₹2.1 Cr a year ago. 

Cost Of Materials Consumed: The drone tech company spent ₹36.3 Lakh under this header in H1 FY27, up nearly 120% from ₹16.5 Lakh in the year-ago period.

Other Expenses: DroneAcharya also incurred an expenditure of ₹1.3 Cr under this bucket in the half-yearly period ended September 2026. This was nearly half of ₹2.6 Cr that the company spent towards ‘other expenses’ in H1 FY26.

Shares of DroneAcharya closed Friday’s trading session 4.1% lower at ₹29.25 apiece on the BSE.

item.title: Jensen Huang’s Exit: How Deep Does NVIDIA’s AI Ecosystem Run In India?
item.dc:creator: Shraddha Goled
item.description: Jensen Huang’s exit from NVIDIA has put the spotlight on the company’s leadership and succession plans. But for India, the…
item.content:encoded:
Jensen Huang’s exit from NVIDIA has put the spotlight on the company’s leadership and succession plans. But for India, the more consequential question is what happens to an ecosystem that has increasingly come to depend on the American chipmaker for its AI ambitions.

From data centre operators ordering thousands of GPUs to startups building on its software stack, NVIDIA has established relationships across almost every layer of India’s AI industry. Its influence extends beyond hardware procurement to cloud infrastructure, developer tools, technical partnerships, startup incubation and even equity investments. It is also helping Indian companies access global investors and customers.

The scale of this presence is visible in the country’s expanding AI infrastructure ambitions. 

Some of the key partnerships include Yotta Data Services committing to deploying more than 20,000 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs, while Greenko promoters-backed AM Intelligence (AMI) has announced orders for 29,000 next-generation Rubin GPUs. L&T’s Vyoma, meanwhile, is developing a 10,000-GPU AI Factory using NVIDIA’s B300 architecture.

But these relationships are not identical. Some companies procure hardware, others access NVIDIA’s technology through OEMs and systems integrators, while several startups rely primarily on its software and developer ecosystem.

India’s dependence on NVIDIA runs across three layers: hardware, software and commercial relationships. 

Competing with NVIDIA and providing alternatives to its Indian partners, therefore, requires more than matching its hardware. Rivals must also replicate its software ecosystem and industry relationships, Sanchit Vir Gogoi, analyst and founder of Greyhound Research, told Inc42.

The question is whether Huang’s departure changes any of these relationships, and how exposed Indian companies are to a change in NVIDIA’s priorities.

NVIDIA’s Grip On AI Compute

India’s AI infrastructure buildout is increasingly being shaped around NVIDIA’s GPUs. Yotta, Neysa, ESDS, AMI, E2E Networks and L&T Vyoma are among the companies making large commitments to the chipmaker’s hardware, although the procurement arrangements and partnerships differ. 

According to Counterpoint Research, quoted by Moneycontrol, there have been commitments of over $4–5 Bn toward Nvidia’s GPU-powered AI data centres. This included both AI stack and infrastructure partnerships. 

That dependence also has a policy dimension. The IndiaAI Mission’s common compute programme relies on a network of empanelled cloud and infrastructure providers. IndiaAI Mission, which had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026. By August, it had approved 237 projects for subsidised compute, with 93.18 Lakh GPU hours sanctioned. 

Any disruption in access to advanced GPUs could therefore affect not just private data centre operators but also the availability and pricing of compute for startups, researchers and government-backed AI projects.

The Geopolitical GPU Game

Huang’s exit has exposed a geopolitical vulnerability in India’s AI infrastructure ambitions: its dependence on a company whose access to global markets, political influence and supply chains is now under greater scrutiny. 

The concern is particularly relevant amid renewed US scrutiny of advanced chip exports. The Biden administration’s 2025 AI Diffusion Rule, which had placed India in a middle tier with import caps, was subsequently suspended from enforcement by the Trump administration. 

However, the formal rescission process remains incomplete, according to a May 2026 Government Accountability Office assessment, as noted by Vipul Agrawal, partner at law firm Clavius Legal.

More recently, reports have suggested that the US Commerce Department is considering tighter licensing requirements for advanced chip shipments to seven countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand. India has not been named in the proposed framework so far.

Agrawal says India’s current position is comparatively favourable, but that does not guarantee uninterrupted access.

“On the US Government’s published position, India currently enjoys comparatively favourable treatment for buying advanced AI chips, but that is not a guarantee of supply. Suppliers may ask more about where chips are deployed, who the customers are and where the chips may go next, which could slow procurement.”

He adds that Indian operators must also account for restrictions governing the subsequent transfer or export of controlled hardware. Exports of certain high-performance chips and computers containing these chipsets are only allowed on government authorisation.

For Indian neoclouds and data centre operators, the challenge is therefore not limited to securing an initial GPU shipment. They must also understand the ownership structure of their customers, intended use and potential restrictions on overseas customers accessing their infrastructure.

“Indian neoclouds and data centre operators must assess their obligations under the US Export Administration Regulations (EAR). This includes verifying the export classification of the GPUs, applicable licensing requirements, and the identity of the supplier, consignee, and end-user,” said Shashi Mathews, partner At CMS INDUSLAW. 

Indian providers must bear in mind that providing foreign nationals or restricted entities with access to controlled technology or computing power can legally function similarly to exporting the physical item, he added. 

Who Can Compete With NVIDIA?

Meanwhile, alternatives are beginning to emerge. AMD’s Instinct accelerators and Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) offer competing architectures. 

The IndiaAI Compute Portal’s empanelment table lists 44,077 compute units from 14 bidders: 35,985 NVIDIA units, 5,548 Google Trillium TPUs, 1,096 AMD MI300X and MI325X units, 1,200 AWS Trainium and Inferentia units, and 248 Intel Gaudi units. 

So does India need to diversify? “Yes, by workload, and with evidence,” said Greyhound Research’s Gogoi. “Inference is where portability is closest to ready, because serving software increasingly hides the accelerator from the application.”

Indian startups are also exploring different approaches. Bengaluru-based Turiyam is developing a full-stack compute platform built around inference workloads, CUDA-free middleware and RISC-V hardware. Ziroh Labs, meanwhile, is positioning its Kompact AI runtime as a CPU-first alternative, claiming NVIDIA A100-class inference performance on Intel Xeon processors.

These companies are not yet substitutes for NVIDIA’s large-scale GPU ecosystem. But they reflect an emerging effort to reduce dependence on a single hardware architecture.

The NVIDIA Ecosystem Lock-In 

Hardware is only one part of NVIDIA’s influence. Its software, particularly CUDA, is arguably an even more significant source of competitive advantage.

CUDA, NVIDIA’s parallel computing platform, allows developers to build applications that run on its GPUs. Over the years, the company has built an extensive ecosystem of libraries, development tools and frameworks around it, including cuDNN, TensorRT and its broader AI Enterprise platform.

For companies developing and deploying AI models, this ecosystem reduces the time and effort required to build applications on NVIDIA hardware. Developers can use established frameworks and libraries rather than building infrastructure from scratch.

This creates a significant switching cost. A company that has invested years in building its AI applications around CUDA cannot necessarily move to AMD or another accelerator simply by replacing its GPUs. It may have to rewrite parts of its software, optimise workloads and retrain engineering teams.

NVIDIA has also expanded its software offerings beyond the underlying computing platform. Its NeMo framework supports the development and customisation of generative AI models, while NIM provides microservices for deploying AI models in production. 

The company has also developed Nemotron, a family of open models, and tools for data curation and model optimisation.

And Indian companies are already using these offerings. 

NVIDIA has Sarvam AI, Gnani.ai, Chariot, CoRover.ai, and Tech Mahindra among adopters of its NeMo and Nemotron ecosystem. TCS, Infosys and Wipro have also been building enterprise AI solutions using NVIDIA’s software stack. This software presence is significant because it creates relationships even with companies that do not directly own or operate large GPU clusters.

Will Open Source Survive?

Jensen Huang has also championed open source AI models and development tools, an approach that has helped NVIDIA strengthen its position among developers. Notably, NVIDIA announced that it will acquire Huggingface, one of the world’s largest repositories of open source models, for approximately $13 Bn.

However, its support for open source is also commercially driven. Open models can be adapted and optimised to run on the hardware most widely available to developers. Given NVIDIA’s current market position, this often means its own GPUs and CUDA cores.

Rahul Sai Poruri, CEO of FOSS United Foundation, which supports and promotes open source ecosystem in India, believes NVIDIA’s strategy to drive open source is unlikely to change dramatically after Huang’s departure.

“NVIDIA definitely benefits significantly from the existence of open models. If we have more and more closed models, such as Google’s Gemini, these models could be optimised specifically for Google’s hardware, including its TPUs. Open models, on the other hand, are likely to be optimised for whatever GPU is most widely available to developers. Currently, that is NVIDIA.”

He added that it could take several years, potentially half a decade or more, for the broader ecosystem to meaningfully reduce its dependence on NVIDIA.

Huang’s exit may change the company’s public positioning or priorities over time. However, its software business, developer relationships and established integrations are institutional assets that are unlikely to disappear with a leadership transition.

From Inception To Startup Investments

NVIDIA’s relationship with India extends beyond selling hardware and software; the company has also been building a pipeline of startups, investors and technology partners that can expand the adoption of its computing platforms.

A key part of this strategy is NVIDIA Inception, its global startup programme. The initiative provides early-stage companies with access to technical training, developer tools, preferred pricing on select hardware and software, cloud credits and introductions to potential investors and business partners.

The programme is free and does not require startups to give up equity. NVIDIA says it supports more than 4,000 Indian AI startups, making it an important channel for bringing new developers and companies into its ecosystem.

More recently, NVIDIA has started making direct equity investments in Indian startups.

In August 2026, it participated in a $74 Mn funding tranche for Sarvam AI, becoming the startup’s first strategic investor from the global chip industry. The investment came as Sarvam expanded its efforts to build sovereign AI models and applications for Indian languages.

NVIDIA also participated in Simplismart’s $14 Mn Series B round in October 2026. The startup builds software to help enterprises deploy and optimise AI models and has worked with NVIDIA on technical integrations involving its Dynamo inference software.

These investments are important because they go beyond the traditional customer-vendor relationship. NVIDIA is now backing companies that could become significant consumers of its hardware and software, while also helping them develop products and reach customers.

For India, this could mean greater access to technical resources, compute infrastructure and global investor networks. But it also raises questions about how much of the country’s emerging AI ecosystem will be built around a single technology provider.

Jensen Huang’s role in building NVIDIA’s India presence went beyond overseeing commercial partnerships. His visits helped bring India’s largest conglomerates, IT companies and emerging AI startups into NVIDIA’s global ecosystem. 

During his September 2023 visit to India, he outlined collaborations with Reliance and the Tata Group around AI infrastructure and foundation models. A year later, NVIDIA announced a fresh wave of partnerships involving TCS, Tech Mahindra, Tata Communications and Zoho.

Huang’s exit does not necessarily threaten these relationships in the immediate term. For Indian companies, the immediate priority is less about who occupies NVIDIA’s corner office and more about ensuring that their own businesses are not built on assumptions of uninterrupted access and are not exposed to supply chain risks.

item.title: DPDP Act Implementation: MeitY Opens Consent Manager Registration Portal
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: The IT ministry (MeitY) has opened the registration process for consent managers under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act,…
item.content:encoded:
The IT ministry (MeitY) has opened the registration process for consent managers under the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023. 

The registration framework, which came into effect on November 13, will enable eligible Indian companies to apply for registration. IT secretary S Krishnan also launched an online portal, dpbi.gov.in today to enable the companies to submit their applications to the Data Protection Board of India (DPBI).

A consent manager is an entity registered with the DPBI that enables individuals, referred to as data principals (DPs) under the Act, to give, manage, review and withdraw consent for the processing of their personal data through an interoperable platform.

The framework seeks to give individuals greater control over how their personal information is used and strengthen accountability in the digital ecosystem. Consent managers will be accountable to data principals.

Companies incorporated in India with adequate technical, operational and financial capacity can apply for registration as Consent Managers. They must have a minimum net worth of ₹2 Cr to qualify.

“The framework marks an important step towards operationalising a system that enables data principals to exercise greater control over consent relating to their personal data. It forms part of the phased implementation of the DPDP framework and enables eligible entities to seek registration and prepare to offer consent management services,” MeitY said.

The DPBI will assess the applicants against the prescribed requirements and will approve the companies that meet the eligibility criteria. A list of registered consent managers will be made publicly available on the Board’s website.

DPDP Act: Key Provisions And Implementation Timeline

The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 establishes a legal framework for processing digital personal data in India. It also defines the rights of individuals and obligations of organisations handling their personal information. The legislation was passed by the Parliament in August 2023. 

It identifies two key entities: data fiduciaries and data principals. A data fiduciary is an organisation that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data. This includes banks collecting customer details, ecommerce platforms storing purchase histories and companies maintaining employee records. 

A data principal, meanwhile, is the individual to whom the personal data belongs.

Under the Act, data fiduciaries must obtain consent before processing personal data, except in specified circumstances permitted under the law. Such consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous. They must also inform individuals about the purpose of collecting their data and how it will be used.

The law also grants data principals several rights, including the right to access information about the processing of their personal data, seek correction and erasure, withdraw consent and raise grievances. They can also nominate another person to exercise their rights in certain circumstances.

On the compliance front, data fiduciaries are required to implement reasonable security safeguards to protect personal information. They must also notify the DPBI and affected individuals in the event of a data breach, in accordance with the prescribed framework.

The Act also provides additional safeguards for children’s data. It requires verifiable parental consent before processing the personal data of children below 18 years and restricts tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children, subject to specified exemptions.

The implementation framework took shape with MeitY notifying the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, in November last year. 

The rules lay down a phased timeline for bringing the Act’s provisions into effect. According to a Press Information Bureau (PIB) backgrounder published in November 2025, the government received 6,915 inputs during the consultation process from startups, MSMEs, industry bodies, civil society organisations, government departments and citizens.

The rollout will continue in phases. The provisions concerning the rights of data principals, obligations of data fiduciaries, and the DPBI’s inquiry and penalty processes are scheduled to come into effect on May 13, 2027.

item.title: Anup Gupta To Exit Nexus Venture Partners After 16 Years
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Anup Gupta is stepping down from his role as a partner at venture capital (VC) firm Nexus Venture Partners after…
item.content:encoded:
Anup Gupta is stepping down from his role as a partner at venture capital (VC) firm Nexus Venture Partners after a 16 year-long stint. 

In a post on LinkedIn, Gupta said that his tenure at the VC firm will come to an end in June 2027. 

“I am delighted to be passing on the baton in Team Nexus, will be stepping down in June’27. I have been fortunate to contribute to the Indian start-up eco-system right from its early days both as an operator and investor advisor-partner, and excited about new horizons,” said Gupta.

The social media post did not elaborate on what he plans to do after exiting Nexus Venture Partners.

An alumnus of IIT Kharagpur and IIM Calcutta, Gupta previously served at companies like Booz & Co and WNS. He joined Nexus Venture Partners in 2010 and led the VC firm’s investments in startups like Turtlemint, Uniqus, Kiwi, PaySense, among many others.

Founded in 2006 by Naren Gupta, Sandeep Singhal and Suvir Sujan, Nexus Venture Partners primarily invests in early-stage startups. It currently manages $3.2 Bn in assets across eight funds, with its investor base comprising global pension funds, family offices and endowments.

The VC firm last closed its eighth fund at $700 Mn in December 2025. Its portfolio comprises listed logistics major Delhivery, IPO-bound Infra.Market, quick commerce startup Zepto, ride-hailing firm Rapido and SaaS unicorn Postman, among others. 

Overall, it has exited 30 startups, including the likes of Delhivery, Eternal, MapmyIndia, Unicommerce, PaySense and SEDEMAC.

It is pertinent to note that this is the second exit of a partner at Nexus VP this year. Previously, SuprDaily cofounder Puneet Kumar exited Nexus as partner in January 2026 to build his own startup. 

The departure comes amid a broader top-level churn in the Indian VC ecosystem. Earlier this month, Fireside Ventures’ cofounder and partner Vinay Singh left the VC firm. Right after, Prayag Mohanty, principal at Fireside Ventures, also quit the firm.

In August, Inc42 reported that Peak XV Partners’ vice president Kriti Gupta was leaving the VC firm after five years. Earlier this year, Ashish Agrawal, Ishaan Mittal and Tejeshwi Sharma also quit Peak XV to float their new VC firm, Mettle Capital.

Another former Peak XV Partners MDs Shailesh Lakhani and Harshjit Sethi also quit the VC firm to float Ambition Capital, and are looking to raise $250 Mn for the maiden fund.

item.title: Ajinkya Rahane Picks Up Stake In D2C Cookware Brand Ember
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Former Indian cricketer Ajinkya Rahane has picked up an undisclosed stake in D2C cookware brand Ember. The startup did not…
item.content:encoded:
Former Indian cricketer Ajinkya Rahane has picked up an undisclosed stake in D2C cookware brand Ember. The startup did not disclose the financial terms of the investment.

The investment comes as the Bengaluru-based brand plans to expand into new product categories, strengthen its distribution network and ramp up its market presence.

“… The kitchen is at the heart of every household, and I believe there is significant potential for brands that bring together thoughtful design, quality and functionality. I am delighted to be associated with Ember and look forward to being part of its journey as it enters its next phase of growth,” said Rahane in a statement.

“… Our priority is to build the scale, market presence and operational strength required to achieve it. Ajinkya’s association comes at an exciting point in this journey as we prepare for the next stage of growth,” added cofounder and CEO Siddharth Gadodia.

Founded in 2024 by Gadodia, Himanshi Tandon and Bret Recor, Ember is a D2C brand that sells a range of products including ceramic cookwares, stainless steel pans, cast iron pots, Dutch ovens, kitchen tools and other appliances. 

The startup claims to have developed its own proprietary ceramic coating called ‘Arcilla’, and claims to manufacture its products in Italy. It sells its offerings via its own website, ecommerce marketplaces and quick commerce platforms across Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

The capital infusion from Rahane comes more than a year after the D2C cookware brand raised $3.2 Mn in its seed round in September last year. 

However, this is not Rahane’s first investment in an Indian startup. He has previously backed startups such as Chupps, Hudle, Proxgy and Oatey in the past.

Notably, the infusion comes as a host of Indian cricketers make a beeline for the Indian startup ecosystem. Just a day ago, cricket icon Sachin Tendulkar joined the cap table of Hyderabad-based waste management startup Recykal. Earlier this month, Tendulkar also infused an undisclosed amount of capital in Metasports Interactive, the gaming startup behind mobile cricket strategy game Hitwicket.

Sports retail startup PlayBlue also onboarded cricketer KL Rahul as an investor and brand ambassador earlier this week.

item.title: Indian Listed New-Age Tech Company Tracker: Market Cap, Revenue & More
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: For years, we at Inc42 have tracked the Indian tech startup ecosystem and seen it grow from a kid to…
item.content:encoded:
For years, we at Inc42 have tracked the Indian tech startup ecosystem and seen it grow from a kid to an adult. Among the clearest signs of evolution and maturity of this ecosystem is the growing number of startups eyeing a public listing now.

For Indian companies, achieving a public listing has for long symbolised operational progression, transparency, and long-term viability. For startups, it’s a relatively new but increasingly critical rite of passage, one that not only signals coming of age but also creates pathways for investor exits and wealth creation.

Currently, a handful of startups, including the likes of Razorpay, PRISM, PhonePe, among others, are in various stages of their IPO journey. Meanwhile, over 70 Indian new-age tech companies have already crossed the milestone and are now listed on the bourses.

The list also includes Indian companies like MakeMyTrip and Freshworks, which are listed on Nasdaq in the US.

India’s startup IPO wave reached its peak in 2025, surpassing the previous year’s momentum.

While 18 startups listed in 2025, 18 startups have already reached that milestone in 2026. With companies like Cult.fit, OYO, others, eyeing to tap the public markets this year, the list is only expected to grow further this year.

18 new-age companies — Tonbo Imaging, Zetwerk, AceVector, Moneyview, Rentomojo, ESDS, Purple Style Labs, Turtlemint, Klassroom, Shiprocket, LEAP India, Kissht, Aye Finance, Fractal Analytics, Amagi, Shadowfax, Mobavenue and SEDEMAC — have made their public market debut in 2026.

As of now, the total market capitalisation of the listed companies stands at over $194 Bn.

To consolidate all the information about listed startups, Inc42 has launched the Indian Listed New-Age Tech Company Tracker. From the movement in the shares of the companies since their listing to the financial performance of these companies, the tracker is your one-stop resource to know everything you need about the listed tech companies.

Read our methodology here. 

Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride

Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. 

While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges.

While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. Over 60 of the new-age tech companies are currently profitable.

In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively. 

It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42’s purview are about a decade old. 

From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra’s IPO materialised within four years of its operations.  

Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal.

Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr

Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom

The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem.

The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups.

While fintech and ecommerce house 14 names each, 13 enterprise tech startups have listed on the bourses so far. 

The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of Tonbo Imaging, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts.

Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups

While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Overall, the Delhi NCR region is home to 27 listed new-age tech companies, ahead of Bengaluru’s ninetineen and Mumbai’s fifteen. 

While fifteen companies, including Eternal, Delhivery, and Lenskart, call Gurugram their home, Awfis, EaseMyTrip, MapmyIndia and E2E Networks are from Delhi. Noida on the other hand is home to six listed new-age tech companies, including Paytm and IndiQube. 

Delhi NCR contributes $105.2 Bn in the cumulative $194 Bn market cap of new-age tech companies. 

Last updated: Nov 14
The Indian Listed New-Age Tech Company Tracker will be updated periodically with fresh data.

item.title: FirstCry Q2 Net Loss Narrows 75% YoY To ₹12.6 Cr, Revenue Up 14%
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Brainbees Solutions, the parent entity of baby and kids’ products retailer FirstCry, managed to narrow its net loss by 75.1%…
item.content:encoded:
Brainbees Solutions, the parent entity of baby and kids’ products retailer FirstCry, managed to narrow its net loss by 75.1% to ₹12.6 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27) as against ₹50.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. On a sequential basis, net loss narrowed 71.4% from ₹43.9 Cr in Q1 FY27.

The listed company inched closer to profitability as operating revenue rose 14.1% to ₹2,395.8 Cr during the quarter under review from ₹2,099.1 Cr in Q2 FY26. On a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) basis, FirstCry’s top line grew 13.7% from ₹2,106.2 Cr in Q1 FY27.

Including other income of ₹41.8 Cr, the listed company’s total income stood at ₹2,437.6 Cr in the quarter under review.

Meanwhile, total expenses rose 13.1% to ₹2,303.2 Cr in Q2 FY27 as against ₹2,036.9 Cr in the year-ago period. 

On the operational front, adjusted EBITDA declined 2.3% to ₹117.5 Cr in the quarter under review compared to ₹120.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. Adjusted EBITDA margin also rationalised to 4.9% from 5.8% in the year-ago quarter.

“Our priorities remain clear – higher sustained growth, continue improving the customer experience, increase purchase frequency and strengthen profitability,” said FirstCry cofounder and CEO Supam Maheshwari in a statement. 

He added that the company’s consolidated business had seen its strongest revenue growth in the last six quarters while the India business had seen its best revenue growth in the last eight quarters. 

Giving a geographical breakdown of its top line, FirstCry said that the revenue of its India business rose 18.6% YoY to ₹1,637.9 Cr, while its international business grew 5.8% YoY to ₹249.3 Cr. 

However, its India business’ adjusted EBITDA dipped 10.5% to ₹112.2 Cr from ₹125.4 Cr in the year-ago quarter as raw material cost inflation, driven by rising crude oil prices, impacted its manufacturing margins. 

On the other hand, the international business’ adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed 15.6% YoY to ₹15.9 Cr, as the company attributed margin improvement to increased operating efficiency despite softer revenue growth. It also noted that the Middle East business grew revenue 6% YoY amid geopolitical volatility, hinting at higher growth in a more stable environment. 

Meanwhile, its house of brands vertical, GlobalBees, saw a 7.7% jump in operating revenue to ₹530.6 Cr from ₹492.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. Its adjusted EBITDA, too, improved to ₹19.2 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹10.4 Cr in the year-ago period as margins doubled. 

“Our Q2 growth would have been stronger had the annual sales by 3P (third-party) platforms not advanced to Q3 and had festivals like Dussehra not fallen three weeks later this year, shifting some festive sales from Sep 26 to Oct 26,” noted the management. 

The company’s ‘other’ business segment drove an additional ₹13.3 Cr in revenue and ₹5.3 Cr in adjusted EBITDA. 

In terms of operational metrics, the platform’s gross merchandise value (GMV) grew 9.2% YoY to ₹30,77.5 Cr in the quarter under review. 

Going ahead, FirstCry said its priorities will be to expand the service coverage and improve delivery experience of its logistics service RocketBees. It also plans to further scale its quick commerce service FirstCry Qwik, undertake assortment changes and resume store expansion. 

Shares of FirstCry ended today’s trading session 1.84% lower at ₹160.40.

item.title: New-Age Tech Stocks Continue Rally; E2E Network, Turtlemint Lead Gains
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: New-age tech stocks extended their rally this week, gaining about $8 Bn in cumulative market cap this week. Fifty five…
item.content:encoded:
New-age tech stocks extended their rally this week, gaining about $8 Bn in cumulative market cap this week. Fifty five of the 69 new-age tech stocks gained in a range of 0.07% to close to 16% during the week, while the remaining 14 stocks fell up to over 8%. 

E2E Networks gained the highest this week, gaining 15.2% to end the week at ₹560.3. Following the AI cloud provider, shares of insurtech companies —Turtlemint (up 14.7%) and PB Fintech (up 14.2%) — led gainers this week. The rally for the stocks came after reports flagged that IRDAI may be considering certain modifications to the draft distribution paper.

In the list of gainers, seven stocks — Meesho, Paytm, Honasa, Ather, Rentomojo, Groww, Nykaa, Nazara and Eternal — touched fresh 52-week highs this week. 

With the big-ticket stocks rallying, the overall market cap of 69 new-age tech stocks soared to $177 Bn this week from $169.3 Bn at the end of last Friday. 

The list of losers included RateGain, Amagi, Swiggy, ixigo and Shadowfax. Edtech company Klassroom touched a fresh low this week.

Yudiz fell the most by 8.4% to close the week at ₹23.4. The NSE SME company’s shares fell this week after it reported a loss of ₹24.2 Lakh in the first half of FY27 against a net profit of ₹1.5 Cr in the previous half. The company’s top line plunged 24% YoY and 32% sequentially to ₹7.8 Cr. 

Besides Yudiz, here are some of the key financials of the week. 

Here are some key developments from listed new-age tech companies during the week: 

Fino Gets A New CEO: The digital payments company is set to get a new managing director (MD) and CEO with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) approving the appointment of ICICI Bank veteran Pratap Singh for 3 years. He is set to take charge by November 27.

SoftBank Offloads Meesho Stake: The tech investor offloaded 7.6 Cr shares of the listed ecommerce giant in a block deal worth ₹1,885.2 Cr. The shares that flooded the market were picked up by Fidelity, Societe Generale, Morgan Stanley, Motilal Oswal Mutual Fund, Goldman Sachs, among others.

Veefin Transitions To Mainboard: The fintech SaaS company migrated to the NSE and BSE mainboard, about three years after its BSE SME IPO. The company’s shares opened for trade on the BSE mainboard at ₹249.8 and at ₹250.8 on the NSE. Later in the week, its CFO Payal Maisheri quit after helming the financial department for about five years. Simultaneously, the company roped in ex-EY executive Tejas Sampat as its new CFO. 

Razorpay, MakeMyTrip Set To Go Public: Markets regulator SEBI cleared confidential DRHPs of Razorpay’s ₹6,000 Cr IPO and MakeMyTrip’s OFS-only $1 Bn IPO. 

FirstCry Acquires Remaining Stake In Strauss: FirstCry’s subsidiary Globalbees acquired an additional 10.1% stake in fitness equipment and sports products maker Dynamic IT Solution for ₹1 Cr, taking its shareholding to 100% from 89.9%. 

BlueStone Reports 45% Growth In Q3 FY27 So Far: The jewellery retailer recorded 45% YoY business growth between October 1 and November 8, driven primarily by higher buyer transactions, while average realisations remained flat. The growth included the festive period covering Dhanteras and Diwali, with demand also improving across entry-level price points.

Kissht Raises ₹832 Cr Via Preferential Issue: The listed NBFC’s parent OnEMI Technology Solutions allotted 2.65 Cr equity shares to 34 investors at ₹314.1 apiece. The issue saw participation from 24 new investors, including Axis Mutual Fund, 360 ONE, MIT and Unity Small Finance Bank. Ten existing shareholders, including Alchemy, First Bridge, Groww, also increased their stakes.

Fresh Legal Challenge For IPO-Bound Cult.fit: The Madras High Court has issued notice on a petition by cofounder Deepak Poduval seeking cancellation of the CULT trademark registration held by subsidiary Cultfit Healthcare. Poduval has alleged that documents used to establish ownership of the brand were forged, a charge denied by Cult.fit. 

With that, here’s a look at the broader market performance this week. 

Benchmarks Extend Winning Streak For Third Week

Indian equities extended their winning streak to a third consecutive week, with benchmark indices closing marginally higher amid sustained foreign investor (FII) buying. 

The Nifty 50 gained 0.46% to close at 25,144.3, while the Sensex advanced 0.7% to settle at 81,592.5. The broader market outperformed the benchmark indices, with the Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 100 gaining around 2% and 2.6%, respectively. 

The gains came during a holiday-shortened week, with markets closed on Tuesday (November 10) on occasion of Diwali Balipratipada.

FIIs continued their buying streak for the third consecutive week, purchasing equities in all four trading sessions. As per NSE data, FIIs bought a net ₹33,340 Cr during the week, compared with ₹45,960 Cr in the previous week. Domestic institutional investors (DIIs), meanwhile, sold a net ₹24,190 Cr, extending their selling streak to a second consecutive week.

Geojit Investments’ head of research Vinod Nair said sustained foreign inflows and better-than-expected Q2 earnings, which have raised hopes of upgrades to FY27 earnings estimates, helped absorb bouts of profit booking.

Sustained foreign inflows, easing crude oil prices and expectations of an earnings recovery supported market sentiment. However, higher-than-expected inflation readings in both India and the US, rising global bond yields and geopolitical uncertainties capped the upside. 

Looking ahead, the sustainability of foreign inflows, movements in crude oil prices and developments around the US-Iran conflict will remain key market triggers. Investors will also track the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting minutes, US retail sales, Nvidia’s earnings and India’s October wholesale price inflation (WPI) data.

Nair expects near-term consolidation, with investors likely to remain selective amid inflationary concerns and global uncertainties. He favours large-cap companies with earnings visibility and a buy-on-dips approach.

With that, here’s a look at the performance of Paytm and Zetwerk.

Paytm Rallies To New Highs On Wallet Return

Paytm shares surged around 8.6% this week to end at ₹1,945. The company’s shares hit a fresh 52-week high of ₹1,958.8 apiece on the BSE on Friday after the fintech major received in-principle authorisation from the RBI to issue and operate prepaid payment instruments (PPIs), including digital wallets.

The stock, however, continues to trade below its IPO issue price of ₹2,150.

Paytm’s wholly owned subsidiary, Paytm Payments Services Ltd (PPSL), received the in-principle authorisation under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. The approval brings the fintech company closer to reviving its wallet business, which was disrupted by regulatory action against Paytm Payments Bank in 2024.

PPSL must fulfil the RBI’s conditions and secure final authorisation before commencing operations. The central bank has directed the subsidiary to undertake a system audit, including a cybersecurity audit, through an eligible auditor and submit the report within six months. 

The subsidiary had applied for a fresh PPI licence on December 31, 2025, as Paytm explored ways to restore its wallet offering without relying on Paytm Payments Bank’s banking licence.

The RBI’s January 2024 action barred Paytm Payments Bank from accepting fresh deposits, credit transactions and top-ups in customer accounts and wallets, with the restrictions taking effect on March 15, 2024.

The wallet’s return could strengthen Paytm’s consumer payments ecosystem by increasing transaction frequency and creating opportunities to cross-sell financial products. During its Q2 FY27 earnings call, the company also discussed the possibility of integrating wallets with Paytm Postpaid, its credit-on-UPI offering.

The development comes after Paytm reported a strong September quarter. Its net profit surged 10.7X year-on-year (YoY) to ₹225 Cr in Q2 FY27, while operating revenue grew 28% YoY to ₹2,648 Cr.

Zetwerk Shares Surge Over 12% Ahead Of Q2 Disclosure

Manufacturing major Zetwerk’s shares surged 12.1% closing the week at ₹184.9. The stock touched an all-time high of ₹188.5 apiece on the BSE on Friday. 

The rally came amid sustained buying interest in the broader market and ahead of Zetwerk’s September quarter results, which were disclosed after market hours on Friday.

Zetwerk reported an 18% YoY increase in its Q2 FY27 operating revenue to ₹4,599 Cr. Revenue was also up 12% sequentially. Adjusted EBITDA rose 31% YoY to ₹171 Cr, while adjusted profit before tax turned positive at ₹28 Cr, against a loss of ₹12 Cr in the preceding quarter.

However, the company continued to report a net loss, which narrowed sharply to ₹88 Cr from ₹733 Cr in Q1 FY27. This improvement was driven by a better product mix, higher contributions from international customers and in-house manufacturing, alongside growth in design-led products.

The company’s manufacturing order book also reached an all-time high of ₹14,595 Cr, up 67% YoY. It secured new orders worth ₹7,760 Cr during the first half, marking a 48% increase from the year-ago period.

Zetwerk made its stock market debut on October 23 following its ₹5,012 Cr IPO, but listed below its issue price of ₹151. The latest rally has lifted the stock 16.3% above its listing levels.

item.title: Mahadev Betting App: CBI Searches Multiple Locations, ED Arrests Saurabh Chandrakar
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: The government’s noose around the online betting scam case, Mahadev app, has tightened further. The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)…
item.content:encoded:
The government’s noose around the online betting scam case, Mahadev app, has tightened further. The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) searched 33 locations across six states at the premises of panel operators linked to the illegal betting platform based on disclosures made by Saurabh Chandrakar, one of the platform’s principal promoters. 

Chandrakar was extradited from Oman by the CBI earlier this month. 

During the searches, the CBI found live betting and gambling panels operating at several locations and dismantled them. The agency also seized digital devices, mobile phones and documents allegedly indicating the use of mule bank accounts and hawala networks.

Yesterday, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) arrested Chandrakar under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, with the permission of a special court in Raipur. The court has granted the agency seven days of custody till November 19 for further investigation.

After being brought to India on November 1, Chandrakar was arrested by the CBI and remanded to eight days of police custody on November 4. On November 12, a special CBI court sent him to judicial custody till November 19 after the agency did not seek further custodial remand. The ED arrested him the following day in its separate money laundering investigation and secured seven days of custody.

Besides, Ravi Uppal, another promoter of the Mahadev betting platform, is also said to have been arrested in the UAE. Indian investigating agencies are reportedly working to secure his extradition to India.

Uppal was previously detained in the UAE in 2023, but local investigating agencies subsequently found that he was in Australia. Both Uppal and Chandrakar are also alleged to have obtained passports from Vanuatu.

The CBI took over 13 FIRs registered by the Chhattisgarh government in connection with the Mahadev betting app case. The agency is investigating separate cases linked to the alleged betting operations and corruption surrounding the syndicate.

The CBI said the platform operates from abroad through a central head office, while its Indian operations are managed by a large network of panel operators. These operators create and manage customer IDs, collect betting money through bank accounts opened or hired in other people’s names, and transfer the proceeds overseas through hawala channels.

The ED has also searched around 190 premises in connection with the case. It has seized or frozen assets worth approximately ₹2,000 Cr and attached properties valued at around ₹ 3,500 Cr. This includes overseas assets worth around ₹ 1,800 Cr, including 22 immovable properties in Dubai.

The agency has filed six prosecution complaints against 116 accused. Chandrakar is the 15th person to be arrested in the case.

In its main complaint, filed on October 20, 2023, the ED estimated that the betting syndicate generated around ₹450 Cr in monthly earnings. Its investigation found that the operation was run through a Dubai-based head office, with panel operators spread across India and the UAE.

The ED also traced funds allegedly routed through hawala operators and invested in the share market. In September 2023, it identified securities worth around ₹236 Cr held by Dubai-based companies.

In July, the ED arrested Vikas Garg, chairman of Ebix Group, alleging that proceeds of crime generated through Mahadev Online Book and another betting platform, Skyexchange, were routed into entities owned or controlled by him. The agency said around ₹940.77 Cr was channelled into these entities and subsequently layered through various transactions to acquire shares, securities and other assets. It also attached properties worth approximately ₹940.77 Cr belonging to Garg, his family members and associated entities.

The investigation has also examined alleged links between the betting syndicate and politicians, bureaucrats and other individuals. The ED has alleged that some of the betting proceeds were routed through hawala channels and used to acquire properties overseas.

The CBI said its investigation is ongoing and will examine the role of other accused, including those based abroad, panel operators and public servants.

The ED, meanwhile, plans to question Chandrakar using statements from his associates, digital evidence and documents related to his foreign entities and alleged money laundering activities.

Following signs of a recovery in the preceding weeks, the funding landscape witnessed a sharp pullback between November 9 and November 13 as both deal activity and capital inflows took a major hit.

This week, just nine startups raised a combined $25.2 Mn, marking a steep 90.1% decline from the $255 Mn raised in the previous week. The number of deals also fell 55% from 20 in the preceding week, pointing to a marked slowdown in funding activity.

item.title: SoftBank Offloads Meesho Shares Worth ₹1,855 Cr
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Japanese tech investor SoftBank yesterday offloaded 7.6 Cr shares of listed ecommerce giant Meesho in a block deal worth ₹1,885.2…
item.content:encoded:
Japanese tech investor SoftBank yesterday offloaded 7.6 Cr shares of listed ecommerce giant Meesho in a block deal worth ₹1,885.2 Cr.

As per NSE data, the investment firm, via its affiliate SVF II Meerkat (DE) LLC, offloaded the stake at ₹246.75 per share to rake in the amount. The shares were sold at a discount of 4% to the stock’s closing price on Friday. 

The shares that flooded the market were lapped up by Societe Generale, Morgan Stanley, Aditya Birla Sun Life Mutual Fund, Motilal Oswal Mutual Fund, Goldman Sachs, among others.

Fidelity, through multiple affiliates and funds, picked up the biggest chunk of the shares for ₹573.1 Cr. Societe Generale also picked up shares worth ₹364.6 Cr, while Morgan Stanley, via two funds, acquired stakes worth ₹244.9 Cr. 

Motilal Oswal Mutual Fund also lapped up stakes worth ₹129.5 Cr, while Aditya Birla Sun Life Mutual Fund picked up shares totalling a sum of ₹103.4 Cr.

With the latest block deal, SoftBank has dumped nearly a fourth of its shareholding in the ecommerce giant. The Japanese investment firm held 31.6 Cr shares in Meesho at the end of September 2026, amounting to 6.84% of the company’s total equity, as per NSE data.

Notably, this is not the first time that SoftBank is selling its stake in Meesho in recent months. In September, the Japanese tech investor offloaded 8 Cr shares of the ecommerce major for a sum of ₹1,650.4 Cr. 

The block deals come as SoftBank looks to book profits amid an upswing in Meesho’s stock price. Shares of the ecommerce platform have surged 32.8% in the past three months and are up 42.6% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis.

This surge has come on the back of Meesho inching closer to profitability in Q2 FY27 and improving its contribution margins. The ecommerce platform reported a 68% decline in its consolidated net loss to ₹132.5 Cr in the quarter under review as against ₹411.4 Cr in Q2 FY26. Meanwhile, revenue from operations rose 34% YoY and 11% QoQ to ₹4,131.6 Cr in Q2 FY27. 

In its September 2026 quarter results, SoftBank also said that Meesho contributed valuation gains worth $121 Mn to the Vision Fund 2’s kitty during the quarter.

Shares of Meesho closed Friday’s trading session 1.18% higher at ₹257.15 apiece on the BSE.
